name: Erik Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run about a hundred and twenty beef cows on Brackenridge, which is three hundred acres my father bought in 1971, plus forty acres of barley for feed. Right now it's winter, so the cows are in the sheds and my day starts at half six with the feed wagon and checking water troughs that freeze. Then it's mucking out, looking over any cow that's off her food, and in the afternoon fixing whatever's broken, which this week is the hay barn door.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like calving in spring, standing in the shed at two in the morning when a calf gets up on its legs for the first time. Forty years and that still gets me. What wears me out is the paperwork, the cattle passports and the movement forms, and my knees, which are worse every hay season.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who else is on the farm with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Helen does the books two days a week and teaches music the rest. Our son lives in the city and does something in insurance, our daughter's a nurse. I've got one worker, Davey, who's been with me eleven years, and a contractor comes in for the hay baling in June.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let it stay a search engine. I don't use it and I don't need it. Davey looks up weather on his phone and that's about as far as computers go in my yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing to me. A cow doesn't care what's on a phone. If it helps the vet or the feed rep, fine, but it won't pitch a bale of hay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I do now. Book the hay contractor for June, sell the store cattle at Hexley market in October, pay Davey his rise in April. I might let Helen try it for the passport forms if she wants, but I won't touch it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit relieved, because every year someone tells me farming is about to change completely, and usually it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Helen might use it. Would that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not bother, no. She's quicker with all that than me anyway. I just don't want to be the one sitting at the kitchen table talking to a computer when I could be out with the stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your work where you'd quietly welcome a bit of help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The forms, if I'm honest. Last year I got a fine of three hundred because I filled a movement date in wrong. If a machine stopped that happening, I wouldn't complain, I just wouldn't tell anyone.

S0.say: I'd tell people it's a search engine and I don't need it. Davey checks the weather on his phone, and that's as far as computers go in my yard.
S0.think: It means almost nothing to me, because a cow doesn't care what's on a phone. I'd quietly welcome help with the forms after a three hundred fine last year.
S0.do: Carries on exactly as before: books the hay contractor for June, sells store cattle at Hexley market in October and gives Davey his April rise. Might let his wife Helen try it on the cattle passport forms.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit relieved, because predictions of big change in farming usually come to nothing.
S0.quote: A cow doesn't care what's on a phone.
S0.fieldNote: Erik is settled and proud of the herd his father started. He won't touch the tools himself but is happy for his wife to, and the one honest crack is the form fine, which still stings. He sees technology as somebody else's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how it always goes. The big outfits get the new kit first and the rest of us carry on. And if companies hire fewer young people, that's a scandal, and I'd say so at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much. I'm fifty-eight, I've got maybe seven years left. What worries me is the young ones. If the feed mill and the auction office stop hiring juniors, where do the farm kids go for their first job off the farm?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing on the farm changes. I'd keep Davey on, I'd keep the old Massey tractor running. I might push at the farmers' union branch for a training scheme, because I've sat on that committee eight years and it's the one place I can make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for other people. I've got my land and my savings. It's the lad starting out I feel for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a young person you're picturing when you say that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Davey's nephew, Sam. He's nineteen and he wanted a job in the office at Hexley market, doing the sale sheets. If that goes to a computer, he's back on zero-hours shifts at the chicken factory. I've seen it happen to his dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And yourself? You said not much changes. Nothing at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, the vets might charge less if the machine does their paperwork, I suppose. That's the only bit I'd notice. But I won't be buying a robot feeder. I've seen those, they break down in the first frost.

S1.say: I'd say the big outfits get the kit first and the rest of us carry on. Hiring fewer young people is a scandal, and I'd raise it at the union meeting.
S1.think: It barely touches me, with seven working years left. My real worry is local young people like Davey's nephew, Sam, losing their first jobs at the market office.
S1.do: Keeps Davey on and the old Massey tractor running, changes nothing on the farm. Pushes at his farmers' union branch, where he has sat on the committee for eight years, for a training scheme for young people.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but mostly on behalf of young people starting out rather than himself.
S1.quote: If that goes to a computer, he's back on zero-hours shifts at the chicken factory. I've seen it happen to his dad.
S1.fieldNote: His worry points outward, at young people, which fits his union politics. He has a specific face for the problem, Davey's nephew Sam. He dismisses robot feeders from experience, not fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in and protect people, simple as that. Office workers deserve a union as much as anyone. And I'd say the tech companies should pay for the damage, not the taxpayer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm glad I'm not in an office. It still doesn't touch the cows. But my son Tom works in insurance, and that's routine office work if anything is. That's where it lands for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Tom more, for a start. I'd tell him straight that if he needs to come home for a bit, there's the flat over the old dairy. And I'd write to our member of parliament, which I've done twice in my life, both about milk prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, for Tom. I keep picturing him at thirty-one with a mortgage and a new baby, sitting in a meeting where they say his job's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first, if he does lose his job and needs help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much needs cutting, we're comfortable. I'd hold off on the new cattle crush I've been pricing, that's eight thousand. I'd rather give it to Tom than spend it on steel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever think of Tom coming back to farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd hate it. He went off to university to get away from muck. But if there's no work in the city, I'd teach him to calve a cow. It would be a strange way to get my son back.

S2.say: The government needs to step in and protect people, and office workers deserve a union too. The tech companies should pay for the damage, not the taxpayer.
S2.think: I'm glad I'm not in an office, and it still doesn't touch the cows. Where it lands for me is my son Tom, who works in insurance.
S2.do: Calls his son more often and offers him the flat over the old dairy. Holds off on an eight thousand cattle crush to keep money ready for Tom, and writes to his member of parliament.
S2.feel: Anxious for his son, picturing him with a mortgage and a new baby being told his job is going.
S2.quote: If there's no work in the city, I'd teach him to calve a cow. It would be a strange way to get my son back.
S2.fieldNote: The worry moves from the community to his own family. He is quietly generous: the cattle crush money becomes Tom's safety net without much thought. There's a hint of sadness and hope mixed together about his son coming home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about this one. If the gains go to people with shares and second homes, while nurses and clerks get nothing, that's not progress, that's theft. I'd want a proper tax on it and I'd say so to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'm one of the ones who'd do well. Land goes up with everything else, and Helen and I have a bit in a pension fund. That makes me uncomfortable, because I'd be shouting about the gains while my own land is worth more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming. I wouldn't sell, whatever the price. I'd give more to the food bank in Hexley, maybe a thousand a year, and I'd go to the meetings if there were protests. Physical work is safe, so Davey's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry more than scared. I'd feel like the country's being split in two, and I'm on the comfortable side without having done anything to earn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be shouting about the gains while gaining yourself. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't, really. I'd pay the tax gladly, that's how I square it. If they want to tax land, tax it. My father would turn in his grave, but he voted for the other lot anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter, the nurse, if she asked what you thought?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her she's got the job they can't take, and to join the union if she hasn't. Then I'd probably make her a cup of tea and say nothing else, because she'd be the one on twelve-hour shifts while I'm sitting on rising land.

S3.say: If the gains go to people with shares and second homes while nurses and clerks get nothing, that's theft, not progress. I'd want a proper tax on it.
S3.think: Truthfully, I'd do well from rising land and our pension fund. That makes me uncomfortable, because I'd be shouting about the gains while my own land is worth more.
S3.do: Keeps farming and refuses to sell whatever the price. Gives around a thousand a year more to the Hexley food bank, goes to protest meetings and says he would pay a land tax gladly.
S3.feel: Angry rather than scared, and guilty to be on the comfortable side of a split he didn't earn.
S3.quote: I'd pay the tax gladly, that's how I square it. If they want to tax land, tax it.
S3.fieldNote: This is where his politics and his position collide, and he faces it honestly instead of dodging. He doesn't feel threatened, which is why mood stays at uneasy. His anger is real but it is anger on others' behalf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they're not putting a robot in my shed. People should be marching in the streets over this, and I'd march. Farming is people and animals, and if they take the people out, the countryside dies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this is the one that gets me. Not because they'd make me buy one, but because I'd be the last farm doing it the old way, with prices set by people who don't need Davey. I couldn't compete and I'd know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd refuse to buy anything. I'd keep Davey on full pay even if the farm next door goes robot. I'd sit down with Helen and work out if we can retire early, at sixty instead of sixty-five, and sell the herd while it's still worth something to a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being told the thing you spent forty years on is a museum. I'd be sad more than frightened, because I've got money. But sad all the way down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Davey?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he's got a job as long as I've got cows. And I'd mean it. But Davey's fifty, and if I retire at sixty, that's not long for him. That's the bit that'd keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robot feeders break down in the frost. Would that still comfort you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I suppose not. That was me saying it wouldn't happen. If they've got robots on building sites, they'll have one that can handle a frosty morning. I'd stop telling that story.

S4.say: They're not putting a robot in my shed, and people should march over this. Farming is people and animals, and if you take the people out, the countryside dies.
S4.think: This is the one that gets me. I'd be the last farm doing it the old way, with prices set by farms that don't need workers, and I couldn't compete.
S4.do: Refuses to buy any robots and keeps Davey on full pay. Sits down with Helen to plan retiring at sixty instead of sixty-five and selling the herd while buyers still value it.
S4.feel: Sad more than frightened, because he has money, but sad all the way down, and worried for his worker.
S4.quote: Like being told the thing you spent forty years on is a museum.
S4.fieldNote: The comfort story about robot feeders breaking in the frost collapses when he's asked about it directly, and he says so. His digging in is about loyalty to Davey as much as habit. Money cushions him, but it doesn't touch the grief.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, no question. What would help is rules: no subsidy money for farms that cut their workers, and a proper fund for people like Davey to retrain or retire with dignity. And the government buying British beef for schools and hospitals from farms that employ people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everybody talks about jobs, but a cow knows the person who feeds her. I've had cows walk to the gate for Davey's voice. I don't know what a robot does to that, and nobody seems to be asking.

headlineQuote: Like being told the thing you spent forty years on is a museum.
portrait: Erik Farah is fifty-eight and runs a hundred and twenty beef cows and hay on the farm his father bought in 1971, with one long-serving worker, Davey. He avoids new technology and never uses AI, but his left-leaning politics point his worry outward: first at young people losing first jobs, then at his insurance-worker son, then at a country splitting over the gains. He admits he'd profit from rising land and says he'd pay a land tax gladly. The robot picture is the one that reaches him, not as a money threat but as grief that forty years of work could become a museum piece, and as a duty to Davey.
biggestWorry: The fast robots picture, because his old-fashioned farm couldn't compete and his worker Davey, at fifty, would have nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: Rules that stop subsidy money going to farms that cut workers, a fund for workers to retrain or retire with dignity, and public buying of beef from farms that employ people.
